segments.text: **Speech: 5**

**Hon. Kalaignar M. Karunanidhi:** Hon. Speaker, in this House, Hon. members Alagiri, Tha. Kiruttinan, C. D. Dandapani, P. Ranganathan, Rama. Sivaraman, Periyannan, Abdul Nasser, Pollachi Raja, Mani on behalf of the Marxist Communist Party, Theeran on behalf of the Pattali Makkal Katchi, and Palanisamy on behalf of the A.I.A.D.M.K. have expressed many good views on this Government's industrial policy, industrial schemes and the conditions needed for growth. They have also constructively pointed out the work that still has to be done in the industrial sector and, through their concern that progress should be achieved in this field, have given further encouragement to this Government, which is undertaking efforts with determination. I convey my thanks to all of them.

The previous Government came to an end after the recently concluded general election, and this Government has now been in office for roughly 95 days. In these 95 days, the distinguished members of this House, who have clearly understood how many progressive measures have taken place in every sector in Tamil Nadu, have offered both their appreciation and advice on how this Government should conduct itself so that it may deserve still greater appreciation.

As far as industrial policy is concerned, in Tamil Nadu there has often been a rise and fall, followed by correction, then another decline and another correction, and such a situation has been unavoidable.

When it is said that Tamil Nadu achieved great industrial growth during Congress rule, large funds were allocated by the Central Government for the First Five-Year Plan, Second Five-Year Plan and Third Five-Year Plan, and Tamil Nadu obtained the benefit that enabled it to gain industrial development. But when the Fourth and Fifth Five-Year Plans began, adequate funds were not allocated for those plans. As some Hon. members here have pointed out, Tamil Nadu could not obtain funding on the scale received by certain northern States; not only that, it could not obtain allocations that would keep it in the leading position, and industrial growth declined. In particular, nobody can deny that there has been a major setback in the industrial sector during the last five years.

The reason is that industrialists, entrepreneurs and industrial institutions wishing to start industries found even entering Tamil Nadu a difficult matter. As Hon. member Ranganathan pointed out, there prevailed in Tamil Nadu an unhealthy, unacceptable and regrettable situation in which those coming to start an industry had to pay even to meet the appropriate persons. Only in these past two or three months have we in the Government been openly meeting and speaking with industrialists. As stated in the Budget and as I pointed out in the reply during that debate, industrialists have now understood that, with regard to industries, industrial projects and negotiations with industrialists, the Kazhagam Government is an open book. With that confidence, they are now coming forward to start industries. In these three months—
Hon. members here have already outlined the extent to which industrial growth has occurred in Tamil Nadu. Industrialists are all praising this as a good beginning.

At one time Tamil Nadu stood in the forefront of industrial development in India. Though I do not wish to explain at length, in a manner of blaming or accusing anyone, why that position was lost, there is no benefit in concealing a truth that was generally understood. When the Kazhagam Government was formed under Anna's leadership in 1967, and later under my leadership in 1969, 1971 and 1989, this Government followed sound policies in the industrial sector. But that practice was changed, and nobody can deny that there was a situation in which industrialists could not even meet those concerned unless they first paid the required offering before starting an industry. I can say categorically that this is why Tamil Nadu suffered such a serious setback in the industrial sector.

During these three months, representatives from several institutions belonging to many countries have held discussions with me, with Industries Department officials and with the Chief Secretary, and MoUs have been signed for the starting of certain industries. You in this House are well aware of this. MoU means Memorandum of Understanding — agreements of understanding have been signed. For example, the Korean Hyundai Motor Company is establishing, at Irungattukottai in Sriperumbudur taluk, a factory with an initial investment of more than Rs. 1,500 crore to manufacture 120,000 cars a year. It will provide direct employment to 3,000 people and employment to 20,000 people through related industries—

as I have already announced. When speaking about this car project, our Hon. member Thirunavukkarasu said that projects begun by the previous Government too have been included in this note. It is true that, under A.I.A.D.M.K. rule, though many projects announced over five years were not completed, one car project — a mega project — was announced at the very end under the name “Super Mega Project.” It was the Mahindra Ford car-company project. The strange thing about it is this: the agreement was signed on 3-1-1996. On the previous day, 3-1-1996, the Government issued the relevant order. I mention this only to show the difference between the Government Order and the agreement. According to the Government Order, projects in which Rs. 1,500 crore or more was invested would be treated as Super Mega Projects and would receive certain special concessions.

Under this scheme, industries started as Super Mega Projects were granted either sales-tax exemption or deferment of sales tax for fourteen years — a concession being given in Tamil Nadu for the first time. Since it was a Super Mega Project involving investment of more than Rs. 1,500 crore, the manufacturer could choose either fourteen years' sales-tax exemption or sales-tax deferment. In most cases, I think they would choose deferment, because it would be more convenient. If the tax were simply waived, when a product worth Rs. 100 was sold, it would end at Rs. 100 because there was no tax. But if there were tax, it would be Rs. 110 — that Rs. 10 -- instead of paying it to the Government—

they could keep it themselves and keep turning over that money for fourteen years. Therefore, I think that is what they would prefer. Such a generous concession was granted. The agreement also stated that if, during those fourteen years, the sales-tax concession amounted to less than the investment, the concession would be extended further. It was agreed that this extension could last for a maximum of another seven years. They could enjoy the sales-tax concession without any limit until the fourteen-year period ended.

As I said earlier, all these concessions were available only to a factory investing more than Rs. 1,500 crore. But when the agreement with Ford was signed on the 3rd, though all these concessions were specified and guaranteed, the agreement did not specify how much the Ford company intended to invest over five years. The Government Order said these concessions were available only if Rs. 1,500 crore was invested, but the agreement contained neither this Rs. 1,500 crore figure nor any specification of how much was to be invested in each succeeding year.

After that, however, this Government — this new Government — entered into an agreement with the Korean Hyundai company. Under that agreement, the investment amount was stated firmly: Rs. 1,500 crore at the beginning; Rs. 2,400 crore by the end of the first phase, that is, within five years; and Rs. 3,400 crore by the end of the second phase, that is, within ten years. These figures were clearly stated in the Korean car agreement we entered into. Further, under A.I.A.D.M.K.—

rule, 335 acres were handed over to Ford under the Land Acquisition Act. The Korean Hyundai company has now been given 534 acres under the same Land Acquisition Act. In the agreement we entered into, the company cannot sell or transfer this land to anyone else without Government permission — that is our agreement. But there was no such restriction in the agreement entered into by the A.I.A.D.M.K. Government. They could sell it to anyone they wished. Because that restriction was absent from that agreement, they even had the right to sell for a price a portion of the land handed over by the Government for starting the factory.

So, after these two car agreements in these three months, another agreement entered into by this Government — another factory for which an MoU was signed — is a glass factory proposed by the British Pilkington company at Sengunram village near Chengalpattu, with an investment of Rs. 550 crore. The agreement for this was signed on 16-7-1996. The Korean car agreement was signed on 18-7-1996. I wish to state that the credit for bringing these two large factories to Tamil Nadu within these two or three months belongs to the members of this House and to this Government. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

A third factory for which an MoU was signed is a project by TIDCO and the Central Government-owned Telecommunication Consultancy India Limited, with technical and financial assistance from a Japanese company called “Kyugi Kura,” to manufacture optical-fibre telephone cable at Maraimalai Nagar with an investment of Rs. 41.5 crore—
and the agreement was signed on 2-8-1996, which I am happy to inform the House. (Sound of desk-thumping.)
Apart from these, there are projects under consideration. “Under consideration” does not mean that they will remain under consideration; it means projects that are going to be implemented soon.
(1) Bulk drug and intermediates at a cost of Rs. 45 crore.
(2) Flat packs and large-volume amp I.V. fluids at a cost of Rs. 60 crore.
(3) Industrial enzymes with an investment of Rs. 70 crore.
(4) Benzyl chemicals with an investment of Rs. 40 crore.
(5) An LNG receiving terminal — a place for receiving and storing gas — at a cost of Rs. 1,200 crore.
(6) Heavy mineral separation and ilmenite beneficiations & rutile production, estimated at Rs. 300 crore.
(7) Saint-Gobain glass project — a glass-factory project — with an investment of Rs. 550 crore.

In “Ithanniyil,” the news I can give after returning from Delhi is about factories for which the Central Government is ready to issue licences. At Sriperumbudur, this Government has recommended that approval be granted to a company called Innoval Medical India for a factory to manufacture blood-collection bags with an investment of Rs. 13 crore, and the Central Government is expected to announce its decision shortly. I am happy to inform the House of this. (Sound of desk-thumping.) In this—

new factory, the Government company TIDCO is to invest 11 per cent. Technical assistance is being provided by BIRKMEIER G.M.B.H. of Germany. Next, approval is also on the way for a 100 per cent petroleum refinery project with an investment of Rs. 240 crore and an equity participation by TIDCO. A licence for this project, to be established by the Pennar Group with Hyderabad and Kuwaiti industrialists as investors, is expected to be issued shortly by the Central Government, which I am happy to inform you.

When our member Mani from Kanyakumari district spoke, he referred to a rubber-tyre factory. Through TIDCO, approval was given for a rubber-tyre factory project involving an investment of Rs. 500 crore. While site selection was in progress, the landowners obtained a stay order from the court and the project stopped. The previous Government took no sustained steps to have the stay vacated or removed. I give Mani this assurance. Immediately after this Government assumed office, we examined the obstacles to starting this factory and decided to change the disputed site, select another site soon on the Kanyakumari-Tirunelveli district border and have the rubber factory started immediately. I am happy to inform the House of this. (Sound of desk-thumping.)
A project costing Rs. 400 crore is under consideration to use the sand available in the Tuticorin, Tiruchendur and Kanyakumari district areas to manufacture synthetic rutile. An Australian—
company has approached us for this purpose. I also inform you that this too will soon be implemented and started. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

If Kanyakumari is a district without industrial development, our district too is similarly a district without industrial development. So, in future, let the two of us compete with each other to develop industry in Kanyakumari and Thanjavur, and let us resolve to develop industry throughout Tamil Nadu as well.

Hon. member Tha. Kiruttinan said that potassium chloride is used as a raw material in match manufacture and that it currently attracts 11 per cent sales tax in Tamil Nadu. Taking industrial growth into account, under the tax concessions we have announced, I remind Thiru Kiruttinan that this House has already announced that when potassium chloride is purchased as a raw material for match manufacture in Tamil Nadu, the sales tax will be only 3 per cent. I also happily inform the House that the notification for this will be issued shortly.

During Kazhagam rule, action had already been taken as a progressive step in the industrial sector. There was already what was called the Joint Sector. In the Joint Sector the Government share was 26 per cent. In the Associate Sector, the Government share was 11 per cent. When the Kazhagam Government had been in office earlier, we had introduced such an arrangement. Thus the Government would invest 11 per cent or a lower percentage. Through this, private companies could function with freedom, without excessive Government control, while at the same time receiving all Government assistance needed for industrial development.
Under this scheme introduced by the Kazhagam Government in 1989, 49 factories have so far been started, which I am happy to inform the House.

In contrast to the manner in which the Kazhagam Government found ways to expand industries, during A.I.A.D.M.K. rule, as Hon. members here have pointed out, arrangements were made to hand over even well-functioning industries to private parties. Hon. member Alagiri explained this in detail here. Ranganathan too pointed it out. The Ariyalur Cement Plant, Alangulam Cement Plant, Alangulam Asbestos Training Factory, Stoneware Pipes, Virudhachalam, all operating under the Tamil Nadu Cements Corporation, sold cement, pipes and similar products worth Rs. 186 crore in 1995-96 alone and earned a profit of Rs. 7.5 crore that year. Yet tenders were invited to privatise this company. If it were a sick factory or undertaking, it would be natural for a Government to think of passing it into private hands. But tenders were called to privatise a factory that had earned a profit of Rs. 7 crore.

The workers went to court against this. The present Minister for People's Welfare, who at that time was Treasurer of the Kazhagam — and remains the Treasurer even today — filed a case and, joining the workers in that case, obtained an interim stay. As a result, the sale was then stopped and the welfare of 3,000 workers was protected, which I am duty-bound to state here.
One thousand workers are employed — where? At the Tamil Nadu Industrial Explosives factory. It began making a profit for the first time only in 1995-96.

From the beginning it had been running at a loss. It was periodically restructured, the sickness was gradually reduced, and only in 1995-96 did it begin to earn a profit. The present Industries Secretary, who had undertaken that work then, was responsible for achieving that profit. Immediately the question seemed to arise: if it is making a profit, can it be allowed to remain? The Government of that day moved to sell it to private parties from Coimbatore — not one private party, but two. I think you know who they are; I do not wish to mention all the names. First, they proposed to sell a Rs. 10 share, a Rs. 10 equity share, for Rs. 2.50. Then those parties, seeing that a Rs. 10 share was being offered at Rs. 2½, asked for it at one rupee.

At the time it was about to be given, just as a Secretary had written an objection regarding the Kodaikanal hotel, the Secretary here too was present and wrote a strong objection. Because of this opposition, that sale too was fortunately stopped. Otherwise, when this Government came to office, neither these Tamil Nadu cement factories nor this explosives factory would have remained.
Similarly, Tamil Nadu Steels at Arakkonam — the steel company — was an undertaking started in 1972 under the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam Government. It is a factory employing about—

one thousand workers. In 1995-96, the value of goods sold by this company was Rs. 87.72 crore. More important than the company's profit was this: the company had 645 acres of land, and a person who had his eye only on those 645 acres said he would buy the company and began bargaining over the price. Once again, fortunately, the workers — the workers did not merely protect themselves, they protected the factories too (Sound of desk-thumping) — obtained a stay from the Supreme Court. Therefore that sale too was stopped. Otherwise, the Arakkonam steel company too would have gone from this Government into private hands.

As far as this Kazhagam Government is concerned, even if such Government-owned undertakings are sick, if there is confidence that they can be revived and made to stand upright again, it will certainly not hand them over to private parties. I wish to give that assurance here. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

The extent to which industries were run under the previous Government is shown by the figures placed before this House by the Central Government's audit authority. The Hon. members who are here now were also here then. What does that note say? By enabling SPIC itself to purchase at a low price the shares that TIDCO ought to have purchased, a loss of Rs. 12.37 crore was caused to the Government, according to the Central Government's audit officer's report. But the information available to him went only that far. In reality, the Government's loss was Rs. 33 crore. The compensation that ought to have been obtained for 58.45 lakh shares was Rs. 46.76 crore. But because these were sold at a very low price, the compensation received was Rs. 12.37 crore. Thus TIDCO suffered a loss of Rs. 33 crore.

**Thiru R. Sokkar:** Hon. Speaker, according to TIDCO's 1991-92 report, on 31-3-1992 the value of one SPIC share was Rs. 210. TIDCO had given a total of 50 lakh 83 thousand shares. Therefore, according to TIDCO's own report, their value was Rs. 106 crore 74 lakh. They handed them over after receiving Rs. 12 crore 37 lakh. According to this calculation — according to their own calculation — the correct figure for the loss is Rs. 82 crore, which I wish to inform the House.

**Hon. Kalaignar M. Karunanidhi:** Even the date must be corrected. 21-3-1992. It was on 21-3-1992 that they surrendered the shares. On the previous day, 20-3-1992, the market price of a SPIC share was Rs. 105. On the previous day it stood at Rs. 105. The market price of the share, the price of one share, was Rs. 105. Fairly, Rs. 105 should have been used as the basis for the sale.

**Thiru R. Sokkar:** Hon. Speaker, pardon me for intervening. The date on which the then Government decided that the shares would be given was 21-3-1992. But there was time until April to decide whether to give the shares or not. Yet when the share price was rising—
without waiting for that, they fixed the price on the basis of a record date at a very low point; that is why the loss rose to Rs. 82 crore.

**Hon. Kalaignar M. Karunanidhi:** The Central Government's audit officer says Rs. 12 crore. According to the information available to me, it is more than Rs. 80 crore. In any event, crores upon crores have gone. That is the truth. When this Central Government audit report was before this House, did any member get an opportunity to speak about it? Could anyone speak about it? (Interruption.) 'had TIDCO adopted this rate for computing the value of premium to be received it would have a revenue advantage of Rs. 12.09 crores' — that is, if TIDCO had taken this method into account and collected premium, it would have obtained an additional revenue advantage of Rs. 12.09 crore, says the Central Government audit report. Further: 'as such discounting the rate further to arrive at the present value was not proper and was not supported by said formula'. That is, in this situation, at the present stage, discounting it further was not proper and was not based on any principle. Nobody can have another view on the fact that it was based on a principle. It was in that situation that the share sale took place.

Hon. Speaker, as far as this Government's approach to industrialists is concerned, the Government should be supportive of them. In the Budget itself I described this as 'Investor-friendly'. Not only that; investors also need a Government that takes decisions quickly. Our Palanisamy referred to this when he spoke. Things must move quickly—

and projects must be implemented, he said. That is exactly what investors too want. Even excessive concessions are not so important to them. What they dislike is being offered concessions they did not ask for and then having bargaining take place in between. What industrialists and entrepreneurs expect is a 'Good atmosphere' — a suitable environment for establishing factories. They expect and want a Government that understands their problems and resolves them.

One of the principal requirements of entrepreneurs is electricity. None of the Hon. members failed to mention it. As far as electricity is concerned, no new investment was made during the last five years. Before we came to office in 1989, the then Chief Minister, our late dear friend M.G.R., had spoken to the Central Government about creating a power station in North Chennai and had obtained approval for it. But the station could not be established because the owners of the land went to the Supreme Court and obtained a stay. The project, which was to have been created at a cost of Rs. 500 crore, was delayed.

After we came to office in 1989, we studied the project and found that a scheme that should have been completed for Rs. 500 crore had by then grown to around Rs. 700 crore. Even so, we decided it had to be completed. We searched for the owners of the land and learned that they were members of the Pannirdas family. We called and spoke to Santhosham, the younger brother of Pannirdas. He told me that they intended to establish an exhibition or fair there in Pannirdas's name, like the Golden Beach, and that this was his elder brother's wish. I told him: your elder brother's wish is—

to develop only that place. Our Anna's wish is to develop all of Tamil Nadu. So please give up that place. After speaking with him in every manner in which it had to be discussed, he had no other way and went to the Supreme Court and withdrew the case he had filed. Within the next week, the then President, R. V., was invited and the inauguration took place. Thereafter, when about half the work had been completed, the Government was dismissed. Apart from the fact that the succeeding Government continued this project, the country knows very well how much corruption arose while it was being continued and how many cases took place.

Except for this one project, nothing else happened in the electricity sector. That too was a project begun by M.G.R., later abandoned, and then commenced under the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam Government. After the present Government assumed office, it has been decided to start twenty power projects, each of 100 MW capacity, through TIDCO in the Associate Sector or Joint Sector. I am very happy to inform all the members here who stressed and advised that electricity is needed for industry. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

Twenty power projects, each of 100 MW capacity, are to be started. The estimated cost of each 100 MW project is Rs. 400 crore. Together, these twenty projects will provide 2,000 MW. Total investment in all twenty projects will be Rs. 8,000 crore. The proposed locations are Manali, Gummidipoondi, Arakkonam, Ranipet, Sriperumbudur, Maraimalai Nagar, Cuddalore-1, Cuddalore-2, Tiruchirappalli, Salem, Coimbatore, Dindigul, Tirumangalam, Vadipatti—
Nilakkottai, Hosur, Pudukkottai, Tuticorin, Tirunelveli and Perundurai. The twentieth project has not yet been fixed. I think it may be for Tiruvarur. (Laughter.) (Interruption.)

These are not the only projects for increasing electricity generation. We have also made a request to the Union Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas for allocation of fuel such as NAPTHA or L.S.H.S., called Light Sulphur Heavy Stock, or Furnace Oil.

We have spoken in person and are continuing to write letters. These power stations will generate electricity and supply it to the Tamil Nadu Electricity Board. A 'Power Purchase Agreement' will be entered into between the Tamil Nadu Electricity Board and these 100 MW power stations. A Government guarantee will be provided for the amounts payable by the Electricity Board to the 100 MW power stations. TIDCO will arrange fifteen acres of land at each location. Since these are small projects, I am happy to inform this House that construction can be completed within eighteen to twenty months and power generation begun. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

This step has been taken as a precaution in anticipation of an electricity shortage. We are not calling people who have no interest and asking them to start these projects; the projects will be awarded through tender. Further, we give the site. We arrange the fuel. We provide various guarantees through the Electricity Board. We give a Government guarantee. We are ready to operate them in the Joint Sector or Associate Sector. By giving entrepreneurs full freedom in this arrangement, many will come forward—
to start these industries, we expect.

After electricity, another major need for a factory is road infrastructure. I was speaking with our Hon. Union Finance Minister Thiru Chidambaram. He spoke to me about this when he came last time, and I spoke to him about it again now. We exchanged views on how wide and long roads are necessary for an industrial factory to come into being. We now propose to widen the road from Chennai towards Bengaluru, at least up to Hosur, and formulate a major scheme to create industries on both sides of the road, just as there is an industrial estate at Ranipet. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

Similarly, from Chennai through Maraimalai Nagar up to Villupuram, and even beyond Villupuram, this Government proposes a major scheme to widen the roads and create industries on both sides. As Thiru Alagiri mentioned, this Government is also taking every step and making every effort to convert the present metre-gauge Chennai-Tiruchirappalli railway line into broad gauge, which I am duty-bound to point out here.

Next, water is a major issue. With regard to water, for example, Cuddalore has abundant groundwater. This Government has both the idea and plans to start many factories in that region. In Chennai, we now distribute 65 million gallons of water. A large quantity of it becomes wastewater and is wasted. This wastewater can be purified and used for industries.

In foreign countries, wastewater is purified and used even as drinking water. When they use it for drinking water, why should we not use it for industries? In Chennai, this method is currently being followed at Madras Refineries, and I am duty-bound to remind the Hon. members of that. Therefore, this Government is engaged with determination in providing all the basic facilities industries require.

But nobody can deny that, during the previous Government, the Singapore Corridor, which had come right up to Tamil Nadu's border and should have come to this State, went instead to Bengaluru. We have not forgotten how rapidly Hon. members and leaders of various parties issued statements about it then, nor have we forgotten the statements of all those who cared about industrial development and wanted Tamil Nadu to be industrialised. That is why our Hon. member Thirunavukkarasu and others said: meet the Prime Minister in Delhi; speak to him. I have written not only to the Prime Minister in Delhi but to the Prime Minister of Singapore as well. In my concern over the Singapore Corridor having gone away, I wrote directly to the Singapore Prime Minister. This is the reply he wrote to me on 19 July 1996:
To
Mr. Karunanidhi,
Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu,
Republic of India.
Excellency,
Thank you for letter, dated 2nd July 1996. Please accept
my congratulations on your appointment as Chief Minister of
Tamil Nadu. Our closed historical and cultural ties make for
strong, mutual trust and confidence which are fundamental for
good rapport between our businessmen. I welcome your
interest to strengthen Singapore-Tamil Nadu economic relations.
Your letter to me is a strong assurance to Singapore of your
commitment to bring Tamil Nadu closer to Sigapore. Since
India's economic liberalisation in 1991, Singapore has been
taking an active interest in Tamil Nadu. One of our three
Singapore Trade Development Board Offices in India is based
in Madras. Today, the Foreign Investment Promotion Board
(FIPB) has approved 215 Singapore economic projects, of which
36 are joint ventures with the Tamil Nadu based companies.
Your determination to put in place pro-business and investors-
friendly economic policy will encourage not only Singapore
Companies, but more international investors to put a higher
stake in Tamil Nadu's economic development.
I look forward to closer relations between Singapore and
Tamil Nadu for the mutual benefit of our two people.
Sd/- GOH CHOK TONG,
Prime Minister of Singapore.

If the Prime Minister of Singapore has written to us such a letter that gives us reason for happiness, the point is not merely that a Prime Minister wrote a letter. I read this letter here to show the Hon. members, who proclaim “an industrially prosperous, prosperous Tamil Nadu and a strong India,” how many efforts we have undertaken in these two or three months to make Tamil Nadu prosperous. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

There is a magazine called 'Business India'. It wrote an article in June 1994. On the cover — in what was stated on the cover of that article — I will say it in Tamil itself: structurally, for starting industry—

Tamil Nadu is one of the best States in the country. All roads are in good condition. There are 4,010 kilometres of railway lines. There are two international ports, one international airport and five domestic airports in Tamil Nadu. Not only that, Tamil Nadu has 4,366 bank branches. Tamil Nadu is a State with 100 per cent electrification. (This was achieved as early as 1972.) Urban development stands at 36 per cent. After saying all this, the magazine reports what an industrialist said:

Says one well-known Industrialist, "We do not mind corruption so long as it delivers the goods. In the case of the AIADMK Government, the irritant is that it fails to honour its commitment for which we have already paid a fee."
The meaning is that corruption itself does not trouble us; the difficulty is that even after paying, the work does not get done, says an industrialist, according to Business India.
Says one Madras-based Industrialist : "You need not cultivate every Tom, Tick & Harry. If you can please the presiding Deity"
- it is enough if you look after the principal deity -
"Your interests are taken care of. But, if you fall out ever, your life is a mess. Jayalalitha's whimsical behaviour has been reported to put off several major industrial houses "

We know that, for any task to be accomplished, a bribe has to be paid. But, as far as the A.I.A.D.M.K. Government is concerned, what is irritating is that even after we pay a bribe no work gets done, a well-known industrialist said; and that in the A.I.A.D.M.K. Government it was not necessary to satisfy everyone — if the “presiding deity” at the top was satisfied, the intended task would be completed. But if, even after satisfying that authority, the work did not happen, it became a serious difficulty, he said. Thus—

the magazine writes that because of the principal conduct of the former Chief Minister, Tamil Nadu lost many major industries. "Although Tamil Nadu's infrastructure is one of the best, Jayalalitha's behaviour has put off business-men. The report states with regret that, even though Tamil Nadu is a State with all the facilities required for starting industries, Jayalalitha's conduct prevented many industrialists from starting industries.

To expand electricity generation further, there is another large scheme. When I announce it, it may appear to you like a great dream. But this is a time when dreams can become reality. When Thiru Thirunavukkarasu's dream — his ten-year dream — has today become a memory, why should this not be fulfilled?

In Gujarat, a petroleum pipeline begins at the Havira port and carries gas through Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and other States, enabling large power stations, fertiliser factories, petrochemical plants and the like to function. That pipeline is a blessing to those States. It serves as a lifeline for economic progress in western India. In South India, which lacks coal, there has for many years been a demand for a similar gas pipeline — a Southern Gas Grid. When Thiru Gurupadasamy was a Union Minister and Thiru V. P. Singh was Prime Minister, at a function held at a hotel in Adyar, I first emphasised the need for a Southern Gas Grid—

and he welcomed and praised the idea and said it would be considered immediately. Just when it began to be considered, that Government fell. The scheme I referred to — the Southern Gas Grid gas pipeline — is now in a position where it cannot be implemented. But for us, without coal, gas is extremely necessary for power generation.

Further, using gas, large chemical factories, petrochemical complexes, plastics, synthetic rubber and gas crackers can certainly be established. In this situation, even if the Southern Gas Grid has remained merely a dream, there are other ways to bring gas here and distribute it. Places such as Dubai and Indonesia have surplus natural gas. It can be brought to Tamil Nadu at very low temperature. Gas terminals are required to unload and store gas brought in this manner. A gas terminal must have facilities to pump out gas arriving in large ships, store it at low temperature, and then send it through pipelines to industrial centres.

The port being built at Ennore will have a depth of 50 feet, and it has been calculated that a large Gas carrier ship can berth there and unload gas. A gas terminal with all facilities can be established there itself. It will cost Rs. 1,500 crore. Up to 10 million tonnes of gas a year can be received there. A large 2,000 MW power station would require 2½ million tonnes of LNG (Liquified Natural Gas) gas. Establishing this 2,000 MW power station would require Rs. 8,000 crore.

Next, a chemical fertiliser factory at Rs. 2,500 crore; a gas cracker at Rs. 4,000 crore; and a petrochemical complex at Rs. 2,000 crore can also be established. The 7,000 acres of land that TIDCO proposes to acquire in the Ennore area would be sufficient for these. Therefore, a gas terminal, power station, fertiliser plant and petrochemical complex — together, projects worth Rs. 8,000 crore — can be implemented there.

Gas can be carried from Ennore by pipeline to Arakkonam, Ranipet, Jolarpet, Salem and other places and used for industrial growth in those areas too. Likewise, natural gas can be imported at Cuddalore or Nagapattinam and used to establish power stations and other industrial undertakings. Thus, by establishing two gas terminals in Tamil Nadu and connecting them by pipeline, we can create a Tamil Nadu Gas Grid. The two terminals, pipeline and other projects together would total Rs. 30,000 crore.

If you ask what the source is for such very large projects, private companies are extremely interested in investing in them. Who are they? Two American companies, one Malaysian group and one French company are holding discussions with our Government because they wish to implement this LNG Terminal (Liquified) — that is, Natural Gas Terminal — project. I am happy to convey this good news to you. (Sound of desk-thumping.)
The notes placed before you also contain references to sugar mills. Hon. members have spoken extensively about sugar mills. In Tamil Nadu, sugarcane is cultivated over 1.8 lakh hectares—

and if all this sugarcane is to be crushed in a manner that gives farmers good benefit, 45 mills would be needed. As Hon. member Thirunavukkarasu said, the number of mills we now have is very small. Compared with the number in other States, the number is very small. At present, Tamil Nadu has 15 cooperative-sector mills, 3 public-sector mills and 16 private-sector mills — 34 mills in all.

Apart from these, while the Kazhagam Government was in office in 1989, two new cooperative sugar mills at Kallakurichi and Gummidipoondi were recommended to the Central Government and licences were obtained. For some reason, the Government that came later abandoned them, and the work has remained unfinished.

On 11-3-1996, the Central Government granted permission to establish a cooperative sugar mill in Aranthangi constituency. But, by Government letter No. 888 in the Industries Department dated 21-7-1992, it had been informed that no further action need be taken regarding construction of this mill. I convey that information respectfully to Hon. member Thirunavukkarasu.

Nevertheless, I am here to remove his disappointment. In the spirit of saying, “Younger brother, do not worry,” a sugar mill will definitely be established in Aranthangi constituency, whether in the private sector or cooperative sector. One proposal is from a person belonging to Coimbatore; the other is from the Parry company. We will see which of the two has the strength to establish it immediately and give it to them. I inform the House of this too.
Information about the other sugar mills is already given in the note book, so I do not think it necessary to repeat all of it.

Through the sugar mills in Tamil Nadu, there is scope for 300 MW of co-generation power. This year, it is planned to produce 80 MW of electricity. In total, we intend to produce 300 MW through the sugar mills. Of that, 80 MW is planned for this year. I also inform the House that all arrangements needed to produce 300 MW through sugar mills within three years will be made.

Hon. member Alagiri pointed out the loss caused to the Government in the sale of molasses by cooperative and public-sector sugar mills in Tamil Nadu. When one tonne of molasses was sold at Rs. 800, only Rs. 600 was entered in the accounts as the sale price and the remaining Rs. 200 was distributed. This is true. Nobody can deny it. It is a fact supported by evidence. One tonne of molasses was sold for Rs. 800, but only Rs. 600 was entered in the accounts. The remaining Rs. 200 was distributed. I do not wish to say among whom it was distributed; nor do I wish to cause embarrassment to anyone.

After the Kazhagam Government came to office, during these two months an open tender system has been introduced, and orders have been issued that this Rs. 200, which had been going somewhere else, must be paid to the Government as a service charge. Through this, the money that had been going somewhere else is now coming into the Government treasury.

Likewise, there has been much dispute over gunny bags needed by cooperative mills. Even when the Cooperative Minister spoke yesterday, he referred to these gunny bags. As though asking what benefit there was for him, there has been much gunny-bag controversy in the cooperative sugar mills too.

For example, tenders were invited for 900 bales, and the Chittavalasa company quoted Rs. 198 per 100 gunny bags. That was the price it quoted: Rs. 198 for 100 gunny bags. They asked the company, “You have quoted too low a price; quote a higher price.” It then quoted Rs. 299 for 100 gunny bags, and on the basis of that re-tender, purchases were made, causing a loss of Rs. 3 crore to the cooperative sugar mills.

Further, the Sugar Mills Federation purchased these gunny bags at a price higher than the price paid by a private company called Aruna Sugars. See how careful the private party was. Yet this organisation, the Federation, paid more than that for the gunny bags.

Similarly, in purchasing chemicals and lime required by the sugar mills, in 1994-95 they bought 15,200 metric tonnes of lime, paying an additional Rs. 200 per metric tonne. You may calculate it yourselves. But in the next year, 1995-96, the additional amount paid per metric tonne was Rs. 439. Not only that: in the first year they bought 15,200 metric tonnes; in the next year, even without necessity, they bought 23,990 metric tonnes, at the higher price.

More petty and amusing than all this is another act of plunder. In 1995, without any need at all,, an order was issued to the cooperative and Public Works Department sugar mills. Do you know what the order was? An ordinary calendar, if produced in the open market, would cost Rs. 9 or Rs. 9.50. Let us take it as Rs. 10. Here, it seems a photograph had been pasted on the calendar. I do not know whose picture it was. The price of one calendar was Rs. 48 — Rs. 48.77 — and it was printed at that cost. Farmers had to buy it. Which farmers? Those who brought sugarcane to those sugar mills had to buy it. If a farmer did not buy it, the Rs. 48 would be deducted from the money due to him and the calendar would be given to him. The Rs. 48 calendar price would be deducted from the price due for his sugarcane.

I think this “calendar” itself became another “calendar.” The three-loop 'ண்' seems to have become the two-loop 'ன்'. That is what happened. In that alone, Rs. 1 crore of people's tax money — the farmers' money — went into that calendar. Thus, according to the calculation I have given, because of corruption of this kind, corruption amounting to Rs. 25 crore has occurred in this department.

As soon as I say all this, Sokkar will rise, Gnanasekaran will rise, and ask, “Why was no action taken? Why was no action taken?” (Interruptions.) I think you have seen the film Manohara. Someone called someone else Vasanthasena; the people who said it are still sitting there. Manoharan does nothing to Vasanthasena; he leaves her to Kesari Varman. In the same way, I leave this problem to the general public. That is all. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

Granite plunder. A new kind of plunder was spoken about here. During Kazhagam rule, on 2-9-1989, an order was issued in relation to granite. Work would be awarded through sealed tenders. Within two years, a cutting and polishing factory had to be started. The court too recommended that this method was proper. Everyone went to court; the court ruled that this method was correct.

During the two years 1989-90, under the order issued during Kazhagam rule as I have described, tenders were invited and 98 quarries covering 262 hectares were leased out. Through this, the State Government received Rs. 20 crore in revenue. The revenue received in two years was Rs. 20 crore.

In 1993, the A.I.A.D.M.K. Government introduced a new provision called Tamil Nadu Special Mineral Rule 39. Under it, leases were said to be granted individually as special cases. Individually. They said each “specific case” would be examined and a lease granted accordingly. The sealed-tender method was abolished. A high-level committee was formed. You know who all were on that high-level committee. You also know where all of them are now. (Laughter.) They were all on that high-level committee. They were the ones deciding this plunder.

Through this method, from 1993 to 1996, for 125 leases covering 160 hectares, the Government received only Rs. 5.12 crore. Under Kazhagam rule, the Government received Rs. 20 crore in two years; now it received only Rs. 5.12 crore. Nobody should forget that, against the Rs. 20 crore obtained under Kazhagam rule in 1989-90, this was what was received. The new policy is already known to you; it has already been announced, and I do not think it necessary to explain it in detail. Within three—

years, a polishing factory must be established. Only with that undertaking may the lease be taken through auction. It will also be through open tender. Not only that: we have changed the earlier ten-year lease period to twenty years. For their convenience, we have made it twenty years. We are confident that through this, substantial revenue will be earned from these mineral resources.

As for these minerals — while I was outside, what Veerapandi said reached my ears — sand too is included. Just as with granite, even in sand, even in the extraction of sand, they did not leave it alone. Under A.I.A.D.M.K. rule, if an application was made under Rule 39 for a sand quarry, the authority to grant the right to extract sand had rested with the District Collector. It was decided that it should not remain with the Collector; the power was taken away from the Collector and moved to the higher level. Because of this, opportunities for corruption arose even in sand extraction, even in the removal of sand from channels. That is why we are following this new policy today and intend to earn greater profit and greater revenue.

Member Thiru Krishnan spoke about the graphite undertaking. At Sivaganga, a large factory can be developed to manufacture products based on graphite. Therefore, we have now created a limited company called the Tamil Nadu Graphite Company. Through it, the graphite factory will grow substantially in the future and a situation will arise in which industrial development in that district will increase—
which I also wish to state here.

The meat-processing factory was spoken about here. Certain other factories were also discussed. Earlier, when our Professor Theeran spoke in another State, he spoke with great anger about the factory proposed at Gummidipoondi, and about several other factories, saying pollution control must be properly maintained. He hinted at it today as well. Several others also spoke. Even Pollachi Raja, when he spoke here, referred to what was being established there — he is smiling broadly — because if he says it here, he can escape back there among the people of his constituency; that is why he spoke about it.

This meat-processing factory is nothing new to Tamil Nadu. It already exists in Chennai. There is a slaughter house — goats and cattle are slaughtered there. When I go for my early-morning walk, I see hundreds of cattle being driven along Anna Salai. There are bulls among them. Here in Pollachi, there are only buffaloes; there is no cow breed. Buffaloes and goats are the animals that will provide meat there. But in Chennai we see cattle being driven to the slaughter house. What have I seen so far in Pollachi? Cattle are driven to Kerala. Why? To be slaughtered there and the meat processed there. Our State's cattle thus go to Kerala and earn revenue for Kerala. In order that Tamil Nadu too may earn revenue in the same way, we have granted permission for this factory. This is not only in Tamil—

Nadu; if I must tell you, there is the Rajasthan Ship and Wool::Federation at Alwar in Rajasthan. In Punjab, Punjab Meat Limited is at Derabani. Deonar Abattoir B.M.C. is in Mumbai — in Bombay. Who rules Bombay? B.J.P. rule. Shiv Sena rule is there. Deonar Abattoir is there itself. (Interruption.) Then Hind Industries Limited is at Aligarh in U.P. Albeer Export Limited is at Hyderabad in Andhra Pradesh. Allana Sons is at Aurangabad in Maharashtra. Arabian Exports is at Koregaon in Maharashtra. M.K. Overseas Exports is at Nandi, Maharashtra. In Maharashtra alone there are four or five. Alana Sons, Goa — in this manner, when meat is accepted today as food everywhere, it is wrong to assume that a factory producing food will cause harm.

People think that the blood of the cattle slaughtered there will flow on the ground, make the area dirty and pollute it. Such fear has been created. It is natural that people and farmers in that area become subject to that fear; I am not saying they are wrong. Rumours are being deliberately spread. But the animals are slaughtered scientifically without even a drop of blood falling on the ground. The blood released in the process too is collected and used in the manufacture of medicines — that is the method followed in the meat factory.
Another matter: Hon. member Thiru Theeran spoke about the Gummidipoondi factory. I tell him categorically:

No factory whatsoever can be operated in Tamil Nadu in violation of pollution-control requirements. I state this categorically. (Sound of desk-thumping.) Every factory must first establish the appropriate treatment facility. Only after we give approval for that will those factories be allowed to operate. Therefore, I inform the people in the Gummidipoondi area that they need not be afraid.

Employment is needed too. Poverty pours down like honey. Because there is no employment. The Government has the responsibility to provide that employment. To give an example: when doing certain good things, some harmful effects can also occur. When we take medicine into the body, its side effects may sometimes occur. If illness comes, we take an anti-biotic. If we take an anti-biotic, to remove the harm caused by it we immediately take a medicine called Cintac. I have taken it. That is the practice. (Laughter.) So, immediately after taking an anti-biotic, one must take 'Cintac'. Likewise, when the disease called unemployment comes, an industry is the anti-biotic needed to remove it. To remove the pollution caused by the waste products of industry, treatment plants like this 'Cintac' are also needed. (Laughter.) (Sound of desk-thumping.) Thus, because the two are intertwined, we have to engage in these measures to the extent needed to remove unemployment, which I wish to point out.
